Boundary to remember: An agent framework does not replace durable workflow state or business authorization.

Security / governance

Purpose: Apply identity, access, isolation, encryption, network, safety, PII, and governance controls at the boundaries they protect—not as one final filter.

Match the control to the protected boundary
RequirementControl / capabilityDoes not substitute for
Who is the caller?
  • Cognito / federation
  • Trusted identity context
  • Authentication ≠ document/action permission
What may they access?
  • IAM + backend/data authorization
  • Trusted tenant / retrieval filters
  • Guardrails ≠ authorization
  • Similarity ≠ entitlement
Protect bytes / secrets
  • KMS / encryption / TLS
  • Secrets Manager where needed
  • Encryption ≠ tenant isolation
  • Encryption ≠ deletion
Private service path
  • Eligible VPC endpoints / PrivateLink
  • DNS + network + endpoint policy
  • Private subnet alone ≠ private API
  • Private path ≠ allowed residency
Unsafe / sensitive content
  • Eligible Bedrock Guardrails
  • Applied PII handling
  • Content filter ≠ business authority
  • Detection ≠ sanitized copies
Data governance
  • Lake Formation on integrated paths
  • IAM/SCP ceilings + approved destinations
  • LF filters do not block direct S3 bypass
  • Permission ceiling does not grant access

Controls apply across source, index, request, tool, and log copies. Enforce access before evidence enters context; verify retention/deletion separately.

References: Guardrails · Lake Formation permissions · Bedrock VPC endpoints

Requirement to satisfy: Protect each data/action boundary independently and preserve scope/privacy requirements across source, context, tools, and retained copies.

What is managed, what can be extended, and what must I own?

AWS manages: Cognito/federation, IAM/KMS, supported private endpoints, Guardrails, and discovery/analysis services supply different identity, permission, protection, or content controls.

Supported extension: Add caller-derived retrieval filters, domain authorization, verified redaction, action validation, and supported safety policies at their own boundaries.

Custom ownership: Own tenant-to-record entitlement, transaction policy, bypass removal, approved destinations, and copy-specific retention/deletion. Test denied cases as well as safe-looking output.

AWS capabilities that fit: IAM/data authorization for access; KMS/TLS for protection; PrivateLink for eligible network paths; Guardrails for supported content risks; Macie/Comprehend for their discovery/text roles.

Exam clue: Tenant A must not retrieve tenant B’s documents → access/filtering before context.

Boundary to remember: Guardrails is not authorization. Private transport or encryption does not establish entitlement or approved residency.

Evaluation

Purpose: Measure evidence coverage, answer/task quality, safety, latency, and cost before releases and during operation. Diagnose backwards using observed boundary evidence.

Which quality boundary failed?
MeasureQuestion it answersEvidence / trap
Recall / coverage
  • Did required evidence reach candidates?
  • Expected passages vs actual retrieval
  • Absent evidence ≠ reranking problem
Precision / relevance
  • How much retrieved material is useful?
  • Inspect candidate noise + context
  • More results ≠ better answers
Correctness
  • Does the answer match task/reference?
  • Golden cases + business assertions
  • Valid JSON ≠ correct decision
Faithfulness
  • Are claims supported by supplied evidence?
  • Claim → supporting passage
  • Real citation ≠ supported claim
Safety / action validity
  • Is content/action permitted and safe?
  • Safety tests + tool preconditions
  • Fluent success ≠ authorized write
Latency / cost
  • How fast/expensive is a successful task?
  • Queue / first-token / total time
  • Cheap call ≠ cheap successful outcome

Use deterministic checks for objective contracts, calibrated judges for semantic scale, and humans for high-risk nuance. Block a critical-cohort regression even when averages improve.

References: Bedrock evaluation

Requirement to satisfy: Identify which quality or outcome failed, in which cohort, and at which responsibility before selecting a remedy.

What is managed, what can be extended, and what must I own?

AWS manages: Supported Bedrock model/RAG evaluation provides eligible automated, judge, and human approaches. CloudWatch and traces record operational evidence rather than automatically defining semantic quality.

Supported extension: Add explicit rubrics, expert labels, deterministic fact/business assertions, tool-outcome checks, and independent cohort comparisons to the supported evaluation path.

Custom ownership: Own reference quality, held-out independence, judge calibration, critical acceptance criteria, approval, and rollback policy. Evaluate source support and task completion separately from formatting.

AWS capabilities that fit: Bedrock evaluation plus appropriate assertions/domain experts measures quality; Retrieve inspects evidence; workflow/tool traces establishes actions; CloudWatch measures emitted operational signals.

Exam clue: Missing evidence, noisy retrieval, and unsupported generated claims are different defects.

Boundary to remember: High average quality, a real citation, or low latency can hide a critical cohort or unsafe side effect.

Repeated work / caching
What exactly can be reused?
CacheReusable unitBoundary / trap
Exact result
  • Same complete scoped input/configuration
  • Include tenant / permissions / versions
  • Invalidate changed facts
Semantic result
  • Equivalent question; same valid answer
  • Similarity alone is insufficient
  • Preserve scope / freshness
Prompt cache
  • Supported identical prompt prefix
  • Eligible model / minimum / expiry rules
  • Reuses prompt work, not a stored answer

Define the reusable unit before choosing a cache. Compare measured savings with stale-answer, access-scope, and quality risks.

References: Bedrock prompt caching

Observability

Purpose: Collect the evidence needed for the question: trends, caller activity, interaction content, or time across request stages.

Which kind of evidence do you need?
EvidenceCapabilityBoundary / trap
Trends / thresholds
  • CloudWatch metrics / alarms
  • Tokens / latency / throttles / queue age
  • Emit custom quality signals
  • Billing alert ≠ runtime metric alarm
Caller / AWS API activity
  • CloudTrail
  • Configured event coverage
  • Not complete prompt / response content
Prompt / response content
  • Explicit invocation logging
  • Protected CloudWatch Logs / S3
  • Not enabled by CloudTrail
  • Pre-mask input may persist
Slow hop / failed action
  • X-Ray / OpenTelemetry spans
  • Agent/tool traces + workflow history
  • Instrument and correlate stages
  • Hidden internals are not automatically visible

Protect scope, sensitive content, destinations, and retention. Correlate evidence with request, data, prompt, model/adapter, and release identity.

References: Bedrock monitoring · Invocation logging

Requirement to satisfy: Collect the right evidence for the question while limiting sensitive retention and linking it to the request/version/caller.

What is managed, what can be extended, and what must I own?

AWS manages: CloudWatch records supported metrics/logs; CloudTrail records covered AWS API activity; invocation logging captures supported model content when enabled; instrumented spans records application stages.

Supported extension: Add safe correlation IDs, version/cohort attribution, missing spans, tool/workflow events, and custom outcome metrics. Enable content capture only under the required privacy policy.

Custom ownership: Own instrumentation gaps, sanitized-content policy, event coverage, destination access/encryption/retention, and delivery monitoring. A tracing switch cannot expose every hidden/uninstrumented stage.

AWS capabilities that fit: CloudTrail → caller/API audit; invocation logging → protected prompt/response evidence; CloudWatch → emitted trends; X-Ray/OTel → instrumented hops; agent/tool traces → observed actions.

Exam clue: Who called → CloudTrail. Prompt/response → invocation logging. Trend → metrics. Slow stage → spans.

Boundary to remember: Enabling Lambda tracing does not expose every uninstrumented SDK hop or hidden model internal.

1. Read the constraint before choosing the service

For every scenario, complete this reasoning chain:

  1. Hard constraint: what must hold? Consider identity, data location, duration, approval, latency, recovery, and delivery mode.
  2. Pattern: bounded request, durable workflow, queue, event routing, agent, retrieval, stream, or batch?
  3. Ownership: does a managed capability fit? If not, is there a supported extension? Own only the layer that still needs custom behavior, then choose its AWS services.
  4. Controls: where do authorization, safety, encryption, audit, retention, and recovery apply?
  5. Runner-up: which requirement does the nearest alternative violate? What change would make it appropriate?

“Least operational overhead,” “most cost-effective,” and “lowest latency” are tiebreakers after hard requirements are met. Separate first visible token, total response time, queue delay, and retrieval latency. Cost includes idle capacity, tokens, storage, transfer, and operations.

Architecture framework: the AWS Well-Architected Generative AI Lens applies GenAI guidance across all six Well-Architected pillars and the model/application lifecycle. It extends the framework; model selection, RAG, and responsible AI are topics within it, not replacement pillars. Use it to review a PoC and production design against measured quality, latency, cost, and business goals. Generative AI Lens.

2. Learn the exam traps by domain

Use the domain recap for quick recall, then test the boundary in a scenario. The practice questions are original, single-answer exercises; the real exam also includes multiple-response questions.

Domain trap recap

Recall the decision, then check the tempting substitute. Open one domain at a time; detailed concepts stay in the mindmap.

Domain 1 · 31% · Model, data, and prompt decisionsChoose from representative evidence; customize only the responsibility that needs it.
Select on your workload

Compare supported models using representative held-out inputs, capability/modality, limits, safety, latency, cost, and Region/API support.

Trap: Public benchmark rank alone is insufficient.

Prompt, RAG, or customization?

Format/examples/tone → prompting and supported structured output. Private/current/attributable knowledge → RAG. Stable behavior still fails evaluated prompts → supported customization.

Trap: Validate schema AND business meaning. Low temperature is not truth or determinism. RAG and customization can combine; assess data quality, benefit, lifecycle cost, and serving support.

Managed RAG or custom layer?

Use Knowledge Bases with a supported store; use a supported Lambda transformation for custom chunking. Own query orchestration or retrieval only where the managed contract does not fit.

Trap: OpenSearch does not automatically mean custom RAG. Custom chunking alone does not force rebuilding ingestion, retrieval, and citations. Extra control adds operations cost.

Search and context boundaries

Semantic intent → vector retrieval. Exact IDs → exact lookup, lexical, or supported hybrid. Lost passage context → evaluate chunking/overlap or parent-child retrieval.

Trap: Preserve searchable identifiers and measure recall. Hybrid is not universally superior. Evaluate chunking/overlap or parent-child retrieval; larger chunks dilute precision/use tokens, semantic chunking is not a universal default, and GraphRAG has a different contract.

Data preparation must be a gate

Validate extracted structure before database/index writes. Apply and verify required PII redaction; use explicit Glue/Data Quality failure or quarantine rules for invalid records.

Trap: A report is not a gate; IsComplete alone does not validate non-empty text. Preserve layout and speaker turns, but do not treat speaker labels as verified roles. Fix detached PDF columns before chunking; check native audio support before requiring text conversion.

Versioned configuration is not a release gate

Prompt Management versions reusable instructions. AppConfig deployment + polling/extension changes application routing. Model/LoRA releases need evaluation → governed artifact/approval → compatible serving/deployment.

Trap: Versions do not prove quality or approval. AppConfig is not instantaneous global mutation. Registry alone does not update endpoints or hot-swap adapters.

Changed/deleted source still appears

Check completed synchronization, ingestion failures, update/delete handling, and derived copies; coalesce/pace StartIngestionJob requests.

Trap: An S3 update alone does not prove index refresh. Check freshness, entitlement, recall, context budget, and citation support.

Domain 2 · 26% · Execution, integration, and recoveryChoose who controls progress before choosing the runner.
Task, workflow, or agent?

One bounded stateless operation → Lambda. Known durable states/retries/approval → Step Functions. Model-selected next tools → bounded agent. Long-lived/custom runtime → suitable ECS/Fargate or agent hosting.

Trap: Externalize durable state; conventional Lambda invocations are limited to 15 minutes. Persistent processes differ from session state; GPU/host needs require suitable hosting. Complexity alone does not justify orchestration. AgentCore Runtime hosts agents; the implementation or managed harness owns the loop.

Dynamic diagnosis, controlled write

Agent proposes → validate scope/parameters → durable approval/action workflow where required.

Trap: The business API still enforces authorization, approval, and idempotency. Bound tool scope, iterations, time, and tokens; a framework does not supply business authorization.

Buffering or routing?

SQS → absorb bursts and pace workers. EventBridge → route events to independent targets; add queues where buffering is needed.

Trap: Queue age, visibility timeout, DLQ, retries, and rate control matter. Shared workers distribute work rather than broadcast it to every consumer. Concurrency alone is not a model token-rate limit.

S3 event starts a workflow

S3 EventBridge delivery → rule → Step Functions. For object bursts, filter keys, buffer, then pace.

Trap: Direct bucket notifications cannot target a state machine or SQS FIFO.

Prompt chain or conversation API?

Bedrock Flows → supported typed nodes/branches. Converse/ConverseStream → common supported-model chat API. Keep authoritative state, validate intent/entities, and request missing fields.

Trap: Flows is not model-selected next-action reasoning. The application supplies relevant message history; an inference call is not a conversation store. InvokeModel can also implement chat with a model-specific contract.

Acknowledgement or delivery?

Immediate acknowledgement → valid proxy response/direct integration plus tracked job state. WebSocket tokens → decode stream events and send to the connection ID.

Trap: Async acceptance is not business completion. Storing a connection ID does not resume a model stream.

Shared implementation standards

Use application/Lambda code for lightweight normalization/schema checks; versioned infrastructure constructs + runtime wrappers + CI for consistent redaction/logging. Q Developer can assist IDE review/edit/test.

Trap: Preserve meaningful identifiers/case; Comprehend is not arbitrary query normalization. Review the actual diff and execute tests; avoid obsolete command syntax.

Domain 3 · 20% · Security, governance, and evidenceIdentity, access, safety, privacy, and residency are separate controls.
Identity is not entitlement

Cognito/federation authenticates callers; IAM + application/data authorization limits actions and business data. Roles Anywhere uses trusted CA/X.509 credentials for eligible headless workloads.

Trap: Authentication and directory integration alone do not establish document/tool permission. Authorize backend scope → ACL/filter → retrieval; the ingestion role does not authorize every caller to every vector.

Guardrails is not authorization

Use supported Guardrails input/output policies and deterministic checks for content risks; enforce tool/data permission separately.

Trap: Schema compliance is not factual correctness. Retrieved documents/tool results can carry injection; safety filtering does not enforce tenant access. Lake Formation filters do not block independent direct S3 access.

Find PII, then verify transformation

S3 discovery → Macie; text pipeline → Comprehend; model I/O → Guardrails.

Trap: Detection is not verified redaction, and filtered output does not sanitize all logs or derived copies.

Private path and encryption

Interface VPC endpoint/PrivateLink + private DNS + network/endpoint policy/IAM → private role-restricted inference. KMS/TLS/Secrets Manager + least privilege → bytes and secrets.

Trap: A private subnet alone does not create the private service path. Remove bypasses. Encryption does not establish entitlement, residency, or deletion.

Permission ceilings and findings

SCPs/permissions boundaries limit applicable permissions. Config checks supported resource configuration; GuardDuty detects supported threats; Security Hub aggregates supported findings.

Trap: Ceilings do not grant access; explicit denies still apply. Config does not inspect every prompt; threat/finding services are not inline content filters or detectors of every GenAI attack.

Which evidence answers the audit question?

AWS API caller/time/location → CloudTrail with required event coverage. Prompt/response → explicitly enabled, protected Bedrock invocation logging for supported calls.

Trap: API metadata is not prompt content. Logs can contain sensitive input, including pre-masking input; apply access, encryption, retention, and delivery monitoring.

One Region, geography, or global?

Exactly one approved Region → in-Region inference. Approved geographic destinations → eligible geographic profile. No geographic restriction → evaluate eligible global/geographic profiles.

Trap: Check EVERY destination: geography labels are insufficient for a permitted subset. Private encrypted transport does not authorize another Region. Source-Region application recovery and retention/deletion of all derived copies remain separate.

Domain 4 · 12% · Cost, latency, and operational efficiencyIdentify the repeated work and measure the actual bottleneck.
Intermittent or stable throughput?

Flexible intermittent traffic → on-demand. Stable measured token demand → evaluate Provisioned Throughput.

Trap: On-demand still has quotas/throttles. Check hourly billing, sizing, support, and commitment; no universal 60–70% break-even or guaranteed lower p99.

Offline completion or earlier tokens?

Supported offline S3 dataset → Bedrock batch inference. Earlier visible output while waiting → streaming with end-to-end transport.

Trap: Check job semantics, record reconciliation, model/Region support, and completion objectives. Streaming is not async and need not make generation faster/cheaper; handle buffering, disconnects, and partial failures. Avoid universal batch discount/latency claims.

Capacity pool or model routing?

Cross-Region profile → broader eligible compute pool. Intelligent Prompt Routing or custom routing/cascade → simpler queries use less capability.

Trap: Geographic controls/source-endpoint recovery remain separate. Evaluate both query groups; native routing has model-pair/family restrictions. Custom routing does not inherently need Step Functions.

Prefix cache or answer cache?

Identical long prefix/questions differ → Bedrock prompt caching. Equivalent questions/valid answer → semantic response cache. Identical complete scoped input/configuration → exact cache/fingerprint.

Trap: Prompt cache hits still generate; check supported checkpoints, TTL, hits, and billing. Answer caches can skip generation only with a valid entry. Calibrate similarity, scope, freshness, expiry/eviction/invalidation, and unsafe reuse.

Metrics, spans, or log queries?

Changing latency/tokens/throttles/errors/queue age → CloudWatch metrics/alarms. Slow/failed hop → instrumented X-Ray/OTel spans. Across-call prompt/version patterns → Logs Insights over configured logs.

Trap: Custom quality signals need evaluation/instrumentation. Lambda tracing alone does not expose every SDK call or hidden model stage.

Domain 5 · 11% · Evaluation, diagnosis, and release decisionsFind the first failed boundary; test outcomes before promotion.
Evidence missing or poorly ordered?

Missing → inspect ingestion, freshness, source versions, ACLs/filters, query/chunking, and recall. Present but poorly ordered → rerank. Noisy context → evaluate precision, ranking, chunk boundaries, and pruning.

Trap: Reranking reorders existing candidates and adds latency/cost. Neither reranking nor a larger generator recovers unseen evidence; preserve relevant evidence when pruning.

Faithfulness, relevance, or task completion?

Invented claims → source faithfulness. Off-question answer → answer relevance/task rubric. Fluent wrong action → actual tool selection/parameters, authorization, idempotency, and completion.

Trap: Citation presence is not source support. Correctness, relevance, and faithfulness differ. Use source-fact/business assertions plus factuality evaluation before promotion.

Trace, judge, expert, or assertion?

Agent failure → correlated agent trace + tool logs/workflow history. Semantic assessment at scale → calibrated LLM judge. High-risk labels → experts with guidelines/adjudication. Repeatable regressions → assertions/suitable automated metrics.

Trap: Persist required trace events; memory summaries are different evidence. Judges need rubrics and human calibration/bias checks; humans are fallible. BLEU/ROUGE overlap is not semantic truth or tool correctness.

Compare before or during exposure?

Offline → same held-out cases/sources/rubric. A/B → live outcome comparison with stable cohorts and attribution.

Trap: Apply prior safety gates and gather enough evidence; no mandatory 50/50 split. Block a release that improves averages but breaks a critical cohort or repeats a business write.

Canary, shadow, blue/green, or probe?

Canary → small live cohort + stop/rollback + gradual promotion. Shadow → mirrored requests without candidate responses. Blue/green → switch prepared environments. Synthetic canary → scheduled integration probe.

Trap: Isolate shadow side effects and account for duplicated data/cost. Validate rollback/state compatibility. Uptime alone does not prove factual quality.

DOMAIN STUDY + INTERACTIVE PRACTICE Learn the trap. Choose the right AWS service.

Pick a domain → try a multiple-choice question → learn the service distinction.

These are original practice questions. Open a question, choose A–D yourself, then reveal the solution. “Learn the distinction” remains available without JavaScript.

Domain 1 · 31% · Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance

Choose models, knowledge architectures, retrieval, chunking, and prompt governance.

RAG vs. fine-tuning vs. prompting

PDF trap 1 · Domain 1

Key services and controls
  • Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases
  • Bedrock model customization
  • Bedrock Prompt Management
1. Try a multiple-choice question

A manufacturer runs a support assistant on Amazon Bedrock. Its private product manuals are stored in Amazon S3 and updated every day. Answers must reflect the latest approved manual and identify the source passage. The team wants to minimize ongoing model-training work. The application already follows the requested response style, but previously correct answers become stale after source updates. A prompt-only prototype cannot access the private manuals. The source set fits the supported managed ingestion path. Which solution best meets these requirements?

  1. Synchronize approved S3 documents into Bedrock Knowledge Bases and retrieve source passages for each generated answer.
  2. Fine-tune a supported Bedrock model on each approved manual update and rely on the customized model for source facts.
  3. Version the system prompt in Prompt Management with manual summaries and retain the existing prompt-only request path.
  4. Store generated answers in a question-keyed cache and extend cache lifetime to reduce calls after document updates.
Reveal the solutionThe deciding clue

Daily document updates and source attribution require current evidence at inference time.

Why this answer fits

A. Synchronize approved S3 documents into Bedrock Knowledge Bases and retrieve source passages for each generated answer.

Use Bedrock Knowledge Bases to index the approved manuals and retrieve relevant passages for each question. Retrieval supplies the changing facts and source references without retraining model weights for every update. Keep ingestion synchronized so the retrieved evidence actually reflects the latest approved manual.

Why the alternatives fail
  1. Fine-tune a supported Bedrock model on each approved manual update and rely on the customized model for source facts.

    Daily fine-tuning adds the training work the team wants to avoid and does not itself provide passage-level evidence for each answer.

  2. Version the system prompt in Prompt Management with manual summaries and retain the existing prompt-only request path.

    Manual titles and instructions do not supply the private passages needed to answer or cite the question.

  3. Store generated answers in a question-keyed cache and extend cache lifetime to reduce calls after document updates.

    Reusing answers after a manual update can return outdated facts; a cache is not the source-refresh mechanism.

What would change the answer?

If the evidence is already supplied and the remaining problem is consistent terminology or response style, test prompt changes and then consider supported fine-tuning.

How the services fit together
  1. Amazon S3: approved manual versions
  2. Bedrock Knowledge Bases: synchronize and retrieve relevant passages
  3. Amazon Bedrock: answer using those passages
  4. Response: include and verify source references
Read the related guide →
2. Learn the distinction

Separate changing knowledge from changing behavior and changing instructions.

Bedrock Knowledge Bases — RAG

Choose when: Answers need external/current evidence with attribution.

Exam trap: RAG still needs current indexes, correct retrieval, and access controls.

Bedrock model customization — fine-tuning

Choose when: An evaluated stable behavior/style need justifies updating supported model weights.

Exam trap: Fine-tuning is not a live document-refresh mechanism.

Bedrock Prompt Management — prompting

Choose when: Instructions, examples, formatting, and reusable templates need refinement.

Exam trap: A template does not fetch missing private facts.

Bedrock response caching

Choose when: Reuse a scoped answer while its evidence and configuration remain valid.

Exam trap: A cache must be invalidated when relevant source versions change.

Managed Knowledge Bases vs. custom RAG

PDF trap 2 · Domain 1

Key services and controls
  • Bedrock Knowledge Bases
  • AWS Lambda
  • Amazon OpenSearch Service
1. Try a multiple-choice question

A team is building an S3-backed assistant with Bedrock Knowledge Bases. Its selected vector store and citation requirements are supported. A document-specific chunking routine can run within the Knowledge Bases Lambda transformation contract. The team needs this routine while minimizing ownership of ingestion and retrieval. The routine preserves section boundaries and adds source metadata; it does not require an unsupported search algorithm. The team can maintain this one Lambda function, but does not want to operate independent index synchronization and citation handling. Which approach should it choose?

  1. Use a Knowledge Bases Lambda transformation for the chunking routine and keep managed embedding, indexing, and retrieval.
  2. Implement the chunking routine in a new Lambda/OpenSearch RAG pipeline and take ownership of synchronization and citations.
  3. Keep default Knowledge Bases ingestion and apply the section-boundary routine to the context after retrieval.
  4. Keep default indexing and increase retrieved context until the document-specific sections are included in the model prompt.
Reveal the solutionThe deciding clue

The custom processing fits a managed extension; the rest of the managed pipeline already meets the requirements.

Why this answer fits

A. Use a Knowledge Bases Lambda transformation for the chunking routine and keep managed embedding, indexing, and retrieval.

Configure custom chunking through the supported Lambda transformation and keep Knowledge Bases responsible for the remaining ingestion and retrieval stages. The requirement is a specific extension, so replacing the entire RAG pipeline would create unnecessary ownership.

Why the alternatives fail
  1. Implement the chunking routine in a new Lambda/OpenSearch RAG pipeline and take ownership of synchronization and citations.

    A custom pipeline can perform the routine, but adds synchronization and citation ownership when a supported managed extension meets the stated requirement.

  2. Keep default Knowledge Bases ingestion and apply the section-boundary routine to the context after retrieval.

    Post-retrieval processing cannot change the document units that were embedded, so the required section boundaries are absent from ingestion.

  3. Keep default indexing and increase retrieved context until the document-specific sections are included in the model prompt.

    Larger retrieval context may contain more material, but it does not implement the specified chunking routine and metadata contract.

What would change the answer?

A custom RAG pipeline becomes appropriate when required query, ranking, or ingestion behavior cannot be implemented by the managed service and its supported extensions.

How the services fit together
  1. Amazon S3: document input
  2. AWS Lambda transformation: produce the required chunks
  3. Bedrock Knowledge Bases: embed and index transformed chunks
  4. Knowledge Bases retrieval: supply passages and source references
Read the related guide →
2. Learn the distinction

Check whether the managed feature meets the requirement before building the whole pipeline.

Knowledge Bases + Lambda transformation

Choose when: Managed RAG features fit, with supported custom chunk/metadata processing.

Exam trap: Managed does not mean automatic entitlement or automatic source freshness.

Custom RAG pipeline

Choose when: Required ranking, query behavior, or stage control is unsupported by managed features.

Exam trap: Custom chunking is not by itself proof that managed RAG cannot fit.

Answer-stage prompt processing

Choose when: Refine how an answer uses evidence already retrieved.

Exam trap: Answer formatting cannot define ingestion-time chunk boundaries.

Expanded retrieval context

Choose when: Additional retrieved passages supply evidence missing from the current context.

Exam trap: More context does not implement custom ingestion-time chunk boundaries.

Embedding dimensions and model fit

PDF trap 7 · Domain 1

Key services and controls
  • Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2
  • Amazon Titan Text Embeddings G1
  • Bedrock Knowledge Bases
1. Try a multiple-choice question

An OpenSearch vector index uses 1,024-dimensional Titan Text Embeddings V2 vectors for documents and queries. Storage cost is increasing. The team wants to evaluate smaller vectors while preserving an agreed retrieval-recall target. The existing index is healthy and a labeled query set establishes the baseline recall. There is no evidence of an ingestion failure. Any new configuration must use a consistent embedding model and vector size for documents and queries. Which plan is technically valid and gives evidence for the decision?

  1. Build 256- and 512-dimensional Titan V2 test indexes with matching query vectors and compare held-out recall and storage.
  2. Switch to 1,536-dimensional Titan G1 vectors for both documents and queries, then migrate after measuring recall.
  3. Keep the 1,024-dimensional document index and issue 256-dimensional query vectors to reduce per-query vector size.
  4. Generate 256-dimensional document and query vectors with Titan V2 and deploy them after confirming indexing succeeds.
Reveal the solutionThe deciding clue

Reduce vector size while keeping document and query embeddings compatible and measuring retrieval quality.

Why this answer fits

A. Build 256- and 512-dimensional Titan V2 test indexes with matching query vectors and compare held-out recall and storage.

Titan V2 supports 256, 512, and 1,024 dimensions. Build separate compatible test indexes for the smaller configurations and use matching query vectors on the same held-out questions. Compare recall and storage before selecting a configuration; vector size alone does not establish quality.

Why the alternatives fail
  1. Switch to 1,536-dimensional Titan G1 vectors for both documents and queries, then migrate after measuring recall.

    G1 is a different embedding model and its larger vectors do not meet the stated smaller-vector storage objective.

  2. Keep the 1,024-dimensional document index and issue 256-dimensional query vectors to reduce per-query vector size.

    The query vectors cannot be compared with the existing document vectors at a different dimension.

  3. Generate 256-dimensional document and query vectors with Titan V2 and deploy them after confirming indexing succeeds.

    The dimensions are supported and compatible, but indexing success does not establish that the required recall target is preserved.

What would change the answer?

If smaller vectors fail the recall target, retain the higher-dimensional configuration or evaluate other embedding and retrieval choices on the same test set.

How the services fit together
  1. Held-out questions: define the recall target
  2. Titan V2: create matching document and query vectors
  3. OpenSearch test indexes: compare 256 / 512 / 1,024 dimensions
  4. Decision: select a configuration that meets quality and cost targets
Read the related guide →
2. Learn the distinction

Compare quality and cost within the actual embedding model contract; dimensions are not an accuracy guarantee.

Titan V2 supported dimensions

Choose when: Choose among supported V2 dimensions using workload measurements.

Exam trap: Lower dimensions can affect quality; storage savings are not the whole bill.

Titan G1 embeddings

Choose when: Evaluate a different embedding model with a compatible rebuilt corpus and query path.

Exam trap: Model migration must meet the same retrieval and storage goals.

Query/corpus compatibility

Choose when: Queries and indexed vectors use compatible embedding spaces and dimensions.

Exam trap: Document and query vectors must use a compatible embedding space and dimensions.

Unevaluated dimension reduction

Choose when: A smaller supported configuration meets the measured quality target.

Exam trap: Successful ingestion does not prove acceptable retrieval recall.

Fixed, semantic, and hierarchical chunking

PDF trap 8 · Domain 1

Key services and controls
  • Bedrock Knowledge Bases
  • AWS Lambda chunking
  • Amazon OpenSearch Service
1. Try a multiple-choice question

A Bedrock Knowledge Base indexes long maintenance manuals in a vector store that supports hierarchical chunking. Evaluations show that short passages match specific fault codes well, but the answer often needs the surrounding section to interpret safety conditions. The team wants to match narrow passages and supply their broader section context. Increasing retrieval result count has added unrelated sections without reliably restoring the condition attached to each match. The team wants a managed ingestion change and must keep the returned context smaller than the entire manual. Which ingestion strategy best fits?

  1. Configure supported hierarchical chunking so focused child matches are returned with their broader parent context.
  2. Increase fixed-size chunk length until each returned chunk contains more of the manual around a fault code.
  3. Use semantic chunking to form coherent topic passages and return the matched passage without parent expansion.
  4. Disable chunking so retrieval supplies the complete manual containing the matching fault code.
Reveal the solutionThe deciding clue

The matching unit should be small, while the returned context should include its surrounding section.

Why this answer fits

A. Configure supported hierarchical chunking so focused child matches are returned with their broader parent context.

Hierarchical chunking indexes child passages for focused matching and replaces retrieved children with their parent context. This directly connects narrow fault-code matches to the surrounding conditions the answer needs. Evaluate the additional context against the token budget.

Why the alternatives fail
  1. Increase fixed-size chunk length until each returned chunk contains more of the manual around a fault code.

    Larger fixed chunks can add context, but change the matching unit rather than providing the requested small-child matching with parent-context return.

  2. Use semantic chunking to form coherent topic passages and return the matched passage without parent expansion.

    Semantic chunking can create coherent passages, but does not supply the specifically requested child-to-parent expansion.

  3. Disable chunking so retrieval supplies the complete manual containing the matching fault code.

    A complete long manual exceeds the required bounded section context and loses the focused matching unit.

What would change the answer?

If coherent independent passages already contain all required conditions, fixed-size or semantic chunking may meet the requirement with less surrounding context.

How the services fit together
  1. Maintenance manual: section and safety conditions
  2. Knowledge Bases ingestion: create parent and child chunks
  3. Retrieval: match the focused child passage
  4. Model context: return the broader parent section
Read the related guide →
2. Learn the distinction

Choose chunking for document structure and retrieval needs, then measure it.

Hierarchical chunking

Choose when: Structured documents benefit from focused child retrieval and broader parent context.

Exam trap: Returned parent context consumes tokens and can change result counts.

Fixed-size chunking

Choose when: Predictable simple splits meet the measured evidence requirement.

Exam trap: A hard boundary can separate a condition from its claim.

Semantic chunking

Choose when: Meaning-based boundaries improve results on the tested corpus.

Exam trap: It is not always best and does not imply parent substitution.

No chunking

Choose when: A small self-contained document can be retrieved as one unit.

Exam trap: Large documents can weaken focused matching and consume excessive context.

Vector vs. hybrid vs. reranking

PDF trap 14 · Domain 1

Key services and controls
  • Amazon OpenSearch Service
  • Bedrock Knowledge Bases
  • Bedrock reranker models
1. Try a multiple-choice question

A Bedrock assistant uses an OpenSearch vector index of equipment manuals. The AX-1047 manual is current, authorized, and contains the correct instructions. For “pressure issue on AX-1047,” semantic search returns other pumps and omits AX-1047 from the candidate set. Increasing candidate count has not reliably recovered this literal identifier. Inspection confirms that ingestion and tenant filtering are correct. The team wants to improve retrieval without retraining the generator or weakening access controls. Which change best addresses this observed failure?

  1. Add lexical equipment-ID matching alongside vector search and evaluate whether AX-1047 enters the candidate set.
  2. Use a Bedrock reranker to reorder the current semantic candidate set before context selection.
  3. Use a larger Bedrock model to interpret the symptom while keeping the same candidate retrieval path.
  4. Lower generation temperature and require an AX-1047 citation while keeping the same retrieved passages.
Reveal the solutionThe deciding clue

The correct source is absent from retrieval candidates, despite being indexed and accessible.

Why this answer fits

A. Add lexical equipment-ID matching alongside vector search and evaluate whether AX-1047 enters the candidate set.

Add a lexical or exact-ID retrieval signal alongside semantic search so AX-1047 can enter the candidate set. The failure occurs before reranking and generation; those stages can only use evidence they receive. Evaluate candidate recall before changing the generator.

Why the alternatives fail
  1. Use a Bedrock reranker to reorder the current semantic candidate set before context selection.

    A reranker can reorder existing candidates, but AX-1047 is not in the input set.

  2. Use a larger Bedrock model to interpret the symptom while keeping the same candidate retrieval path.

    The larger model still receives other manuals rather than the private AX-1047 instructions.

  3. Lower generation temperature and require an AX-1047 citation while keeping the same retrieved passages.

    More consistent generation does not correct the missing retrieval candidate.

What would change the answer?

If AX-1047 enters the candidate set but ranks below irrelevant passages, reranking becomes a reasonable next experiment.

How the services fit together
  1. User question: AX-1047 plus the pressure symptom
  2. OpenSearch: combine literal-ID and semantic candidate retrieval
  3. Candidate check: confirm the AX-1047 passage is present
  4. Amazon Bedrock: answer from the selected authorized passage
Read the related guide →
2. Learn the distinction

Retrieval collects candidates; reranking reorders candidates it actually receives.

OpenSearch lexical / vector retrieval

Choose when: Literal identifiers and semantic intent both need to influence candidate selection.

Exam trap: Hybrid support/configuration matters; it is not universally higher quality.

Bedrock reranking

Choose when: The relevant evidence is already in a broad candidate set but poorly ordered.

Exam trap: A reranker cannot recover a document absent from its input.

Bedrock generation model

Choose when: Generation capability is the measured bottleneck with adequate evidence.

Exam trap: A stronger model cannot supply a missing private passage.

Inference parameter tuning

Choose when: Tune sampling when generation variability is the measured defect.

Exam trap: Sampling parameters do not retrieve an omitted private source.

Prompt Management vs. Flows vs. workflow

Domain 1 trap summary · PDF pp. 5–8

Key services and controls
  • Bedrock Prompt Management
  • Amazon Bedrock Flows
  • AWS Step Functions
1. Try a multiple-choice question

Three applications invoke Amazon Bedrock using shared prompt templates. Releases must identify the exact template version, variable definitions, and model configuration used. The team wants centralized template management and reproducible releases. Each application currently copies prompt text into its code, so template changes require three separate releases and past evaluations are hard to reproduce. No long-running approval wait or multi-node invocation chain is part of this requirement. Which capability is the most direct fit?

  1. Publish shared prompt resources and approved versions through Bedrock Prompt Management and reference them from the applications.
  2. Create a Bedrock Flow for each application and keep prompt definitions separately inside those flow nodes.
  3. Record prompt text in Step Functions execution inputs and use execution history to reproduce prior application releases.
  4. Enable model invocation logging and use logged requests to reconstruct the prompt configuration used by each application.
Reveal the solutionThe deciding clue

The shared resource is a versioned prompt template and its invocation configuration.

Why this answer fits

A. Publish shared prompt resources and approved versions through Bedrock Prompt Management and reference them from the applications.

Bedrock Prompt Management stores reusable templates, variables, and supported configuration, and creates versions that applications can reference. This supplies a common released prompt resource rather than introducing a new runtime workflow. Evaluate a version before promoting it.

Why the alternatives fail
  1. Create a Bedrock Flow for each application and keep prompt definitions separately inside those flow nodes.

    Flows connect execution nodes; the stated requirement is governance of reusable prompt resources, not a node execution chain.

  2. Record prompt text in Step Functions execution inputs and use execution history to reproduce prior application releases.

    Execution history records a process run, rather than managing the shared prompt template and released variants.

  3. Enable model invocation logging and use logged requests to reconstruct the prompt configuration used by each application.

    Logs help investigate calls, but do not manage reusable templates and release versions.

What would change the answer?

Use Bedrock Flows when the requirement becomes a supported visual chain of prompts, retrieval, and conditions; use Step Functions for durable business steps and waits.

How the services fit together
  1. Shared template: variables and model configuration
  2. Bedrock Prompt Management: create a released version
  3. Release evaluation: approve the version
  4. Applications: reference the approved prompt version
Read the related guide →
2. Learn the distinction

Template governance, visual prompt chains, and durable business orchestration have different owners.

Bedrock Prompt Management

Choose when: Store and version prompt templates and their configuration.

Exam trap: A saved version is not evidence that it passed review or evaluation.

Amazon Bedrock Flows

Choose when: Connect supported prompt, knowledge, tool, and condition nodes.

Exam trap: Orchestrating nodes is a different requirement from a template repository.

AWS Step Functions

Choose when: Own durable steps, retries, waits, and controlled business actions.

Exam trap: Do not add durable execution state without a workflow need.

Invocation logging

Choose when: Use invocation logs to inspect supported model interactions.

Exam trap: Observed requests are not a governed template repository.

Domain 2 · 26% · Implementation and Integration

Distinguish agents, workflows, MCP hosting, model deployment, API delivery, and shared gateways.

Agents and frameworks vs. Step Functions

PDF trap 3 · Domain 2

Key services and controls
  • Amazon Bedrock Agents
  • Strands Agents / AWS Agent Squad
  • AWS Step Functions
1. Try a multiple-choice question

An application processes contracts stored in Amazon S3. Every contract follows a defined sequence: extract text, run two checks, obtain a lawyer’s approval, then create a case through an API. Approval can take several hours. Failed checks must be retried individually without restarting completed steps. The case API can safely handle an idempotency key. The checks may invoke Bedrock, but the model must not choose the process order or bypass approval. The team needs a record of the state reached by each contract. Which component should own this process?

  1. Use Step Functions Standard task states, scoped retries, and a callback approval state before the idempotent case write.
  2. Use Bedrock Agents action groups for extraction, checks, and case creation, with approval progress held in conversation context.
  3. Coordinate specialist agents in an agent framework and use their conversation transcripts to resume the contract process.
  4. Run the sequence in Lambda and keep the invocation waiting until the lawyer responds before creating the case.
Reveal the solutionThe deciding clue

The sequence is predetermined and must retain execution state across a long approval wait.

Why this answer fits

A. Use Step Functions Standard task states, scoped retries, and a callback approval state before the idempotent case write.

A Step Functions Standard workflow can represent the fixed states, retry failed tasks, and wait for an approval callback. Bedrock can perform the bounded model checks inside that workflow. The orchestration requirement is durable state and explicit control flow, rather than model-selected actions.

Why the alternatives fail
  1. Use Bedrock Agents action groups for extraction, checks, and case creation, with approval progress held in conversation context.

    Conversation context is not the durable workflow and callback mechanism needed for the prescribed approval process.

  2. Coordinate specialist agents in an agent framework and use their conversation transcripts to resume the contract process.

    Specialist coordination does not itself supply durable execution state and per-step recovery for the fixed process.

  3. Run the sequence in Lambda and keep the invocation waiting until the lawyer responds before creating the case.

    The approval can exceed Lambda execution limits and keeps a task running instead of persisting a durable wait.

What would change the answer?

An agent becomes appropriate when the next permitted tool or action genuinely depends on model reasoning over observations, rather than a known sequence.

How the services fit together
  1. Step Functions Standard: start the contract execution
  2. Extraction and Bedrock tasks: run the defined checks
  3. Approval callback: wait for the lawyer’s decision
  4. Case API task: create the approved case with idempotency protection
Read the related guide →
2. Learn the distinction

Ask who chooses the next action: the model or developer-defined workflow states.

Step Functions Standard

Choose when: Known control flow must survive waits and partial failures.

Exam trap: Durability does not make repeated external writes safe without idempotency.

Bedrock Agents

Choose when: An FM must decide which permitted tool/action comes next from observations.

Exam trap: Fixed steps do not require model-selected autonomy.

Agent frameworks

Choose when: Custom agent logic or specialist coordination is required.

Exam trap: Framework choice does not replace deterministic approval/authorization.

Long-running Lambda

Choose when: Use Lambda for bounded tasks within a process.

Exam trap: A Lambda invocation is not an hours-long approval wait.

Synchronous vs. streaming vs. asynchronous

PDF trap 4 · Domain 2

Key services and controls
  • Bedrock Converse / ConverseStream
  • Amazon API Gateway
  • Amazon SQS
1. Try a multiple-choice question

A writing assistant calls Amazon Bedrock through an API Gateway REST API and Lambda. The current path buffers the complete answer. Users accept the total generation time but want text to appear as it is generated. The selected model and integrations support streaming. Traces show neither initialization delay nor model throttling. The user must remain in the writing session, and the application must retain its authenticated REST API entry point. Which change best meets the user requirement?

  1. Use ConverseStream and forward output through Lambda and the API Gateway REST streaming integration as it arrives.
  2. Retain Converse and buffered Lambda output, but increase the API Gateway integration timeout for longer responses.
  3. Queue requests in SQS, return a job identifier, and let the client retrieve the completed answer from a result endpoint.
  4. Increase Lambda reserved concurrency and preserve the existing buffered model-response integration.
Reveal the solutionThe deciding clue

The target is earlier visible text, rather than a longer timeout or later job completion.

Why this answer fits

A. Use ConverseStream and forward output through Lambda and the API Gateway REST streaming integration as it arrives.

Use ConverseStream and forward its output through Lambda and the API Gateway streaming integration without collecting the full answer first. This exposes generated text while generation continues. Increasing the timeout still returns one completed answer; a background job changes the interaction instead of delivering a live stream.

Why the alternatives fail
  1. Retain Converse and buffered Lambda output, but increase the API Gateway integration timeout for longer responses.

    The response remains buffered until generation completes, so the first visible text does not arrive earlier.

  2. Queue requests in SQS, return a job identifier, and let the client retrieve the completed answer from a result endpoint.

    A job ID fits deferred completion, but it does not deliver the requested live generated text in this session.

  3. Increase Lambda reserved concurrency and preserve the existing buffered model-response integration.

    More concurrent invocations do not make a single buffered answer visible before completion.

What would change the answer?

If the caller can leave and collect the result later, an SQS-backed asynchronous job is appropriate; if it needs one short complete answer, buffered synchronous delivery may suffice.

How the services fit together
  1. Bedrock ConverseStream: produce incremental output
  2. Lambda: forward events without full-response buffering
  3. API Gateway REST API: stream the integration response
  4. Client: display text as it arrives
Read the related guide →
2. Learn the distinction

Separate complete-response delivery, incremental delivery, and background job completion.

ConverseStream / InvokeModelWithResponseStream + streaming transport

Choose when: Interactive users benefit from incremental output.

Exam trap: Streaming does not inherently reduce total inference work or token cost.

Converse / InvokeModel with a longer buffered timeout

Choose when: The consumer needs the complete response before acting.

Exam trap: A bigger timeout does not expose partial tokens.

SQS → worker → stored asynchronous result

Choose when: The caller can accept a job ID and complete later.

Exam trap: Background completion is not incremental output to a waiting writer.

Lambda concurrency tuning

Choose when: Use concurrency controls to address execution admission and capacity.

Exam trap: Concurrency does not change response delivery semantics.

Bedrock capacity vs. SageMaker hosting

PDF trap 6 · Domain 2

Key services and controls
  • Bedrock on-demand
  • Bedrock Provisioned Throughput
  • Bedrock cross-Region inference
  • Amazon SageMaker AI
1. Try a multiple-choice question

A team has a fine-tuned model artifact and a compatible serving container. Its deployment must use a chosen GPU instance family, expose the container’s runtime configuration, and scale the endpoint’s instance count with demand. The model has already passed its quality evaluation. The constraint comes from its runtime dependencies and hardware selection, rather than a need for cross-Region capacity. The team accepts responsibility for endpoint deployment and capacity management. Which AWS hosting option best meets these requirements?

  1. Deploy the compatible container and artifact to a SageMaker real-time endpoint with selected instances and endpoint autoscaling.
  2. Use an eligible Bedrock custom-model on-demand deployment to avoid managing a serving endpoint.
  3. Reserve supported Bedrock model capacity with Provisioned Throughput to handle sustained inference demand.
  4. Use a supported Bedrock cross-Region inference profile to distribute requests across eligible regional model capacity.
Reveal the solutionThe deciding clue

The decisive requirements are serving-container, GPU-instance, and endpoint-scaling control.

Why this answer fits

A. Deploy the compatible container and artifact to a SageMaker real-time endpoint with selected instances and endpoint autoscaling.

A SageMaker AI real-time endpoint exposes the model/container and instance configuration and supports endpoint autoscaling. Choose it because those hosting controls are required. Having customized weights alone would not establish the choice, because eligible custom models can also be used in Bedrock.

Why the alternatives fail
  1. Use an eligible Bedrock custom-model on-demand deployment to avoid managing a serving endpoint.

    Managed Bedrock inference avoids endpoint operations, but does not expose the selected GPU fleet and serving-container configuration required here.

  2. Reserve supported Bedrock model capacity with Provisioned Throughput to handle sustained inference demand.

    Reserved model throughput addresses capacity planning, not the required container runtime and endpoint instance-count controls.

  3. Use a supported Bedrock cross-Region inference profile to distribute requests across eligible regional model capacity.

    Broader regional inference capacity does not supply the requested GPU/container hosting controls.

What would change the answer?

If managed model inference meets the runtime requirements and the team does not need instance/container control, evaluate an eligible Bedrock deployment and its capacity options.

How the services fit together
  1. Model artifact and container: define the serving runtime
  2. SageMaker endpoint configuration: select supported GPU instances
  3. Real-time endpoint: serve requests
  4. Endpoint autoscaling: adjust the eligible instance count
Read the related guide →
2. Learn the distinction

Deployment follows capacity and hosting controls, not merely whether weights are customized.

SageMaker AI real-time endpoint

Choose when: Serving container, supported instance/GPU selection, and endpoint scaling are decisive.

Exam trap: Owning an endpoint adds capacity, deployment, and operations responsibilities.

Bedrock on-demand

Choose when: Managed model inference without endpoint instance management fits.

Exam trap: Eligible imported/custom models exist; hardware control is still a separate boundary.

Bedrock Provisioned Throughput

Choose when: Supported models need reserved, measured sustained model capacity.

Exam trap: Reserved Bedrock capacity is not a user-chosen SageMaker GPU fleet.

Bedrock cross-Region inference

Choose when: Use supported profiles to route inference across eligible Regions.

Exam trap: Regional routing does not expose hardware or container management.

Lambda vs. ECS for MCP servers

PDF trap 11 · Domain 2

Key services and controls
  • AWS Lambda
  • Amazon ECS / AWS Fargate
  • Amazon DynamoDB
1. Try a multiple-choice question

An agent uses two MCP tools. One tool is a CPU-based service that maintains connections across calls and must remain continuously available. The other performs a short stateless lookup in DynamoDB and has intermittent demand. The team wants to avoid maintaining a service fleet for the lookup. Both tools use supported CPU runtimes and can store durable data outside process memory. A conversation session may call either tool several times, and its durable state is stored in DynamoDB. Which hosting design best fits?

  1. Host the persistent CPU tool as an ECS/Fargate service and run the intermittent stateless lookup handler in Lambda.
  2. Run both handlers in Lambda, externalize session data in DynamoDB, and depend on environment reuse for connection persistence.
  3. Host both handlers as ECS services and externalize their durable session data in DynamoDB.
  4. Host the lookup in Lambda and invoke a new short-lived Fargate task for every call to the persistent tool.
Reveal the solutionThe deciding clue

One tool requires a persistent service lifecycle; the other is a bounded stateless operation.

Why this answer fits

A. Host the persistent CPU tool as an ECS/Fargate service and run the intermittent stateless lookup handler in Lambda.

Host the persistent CPU tool in an ECS/Fargate service and the short lookup handler in Lambda. This assigns each tool the runtime it needs while avoiding a continuously running fleet for the lookup. Store durable business state in DynamoDB rather than relying on handler memory.

Why the alternatives fail
  1. Run both handlers in Lambda, externalize session data in DynamoDB, and depend on environment reuse for connection persistence.

    External data is appropriate, but Lambda environment reuse does not guarantee the continuous service/connection lifecycle required by the persistent tool.

  2. Host both handlers as ECS services and externalize their durable session data in DynamoDB.

    Both tools can run in containers, but the lookup then retains the service fleet the team wants to avoid.

  3. Host the lookup in Lambda and invoke a new short-lived Fargate task for every call to the persistent tool.

    Fargate supports the runtime, but launching a fresh task for each call does not maintain the required continuously available tool service.

What would change the answer?

If both handlers become short stateless operations, Lambda can fit both; if the lookup gains a persistent runtime requirement, reconsider container hosting.

How the services fit together

MCP client: route calls to the requested tool

Tools have different runtime requirements

  • ECS / Fargate: maintain the persistent CPU tool service
  • AWS Lambda: execute the short lookup on demand

Amazon DynamoDB: hold durable business data outside handler memory

Read the related guide →
2. Learn the distinction

Choose hosting by tool runtime, duration, dependencies, and service lifecycle.

ECS / Fargate + Lambda

Choose when: Different runtime profiles justify separate hosting choices.

Exam trap: Check runtime support; GPU/host-specific needs can require another compute choice.

Lambda execution environment

Choose when: Bounded stateless tool handlers fit Lambda.

Exam trap: Invocation memory is not a continuously available durable service contract.

ECS services

Choose when: A persistent runtime is needed and service operations are justified.

Exam trap: External DynamoDB state alone does not force containers.

Fargate task per call

Choose when: A bounded container task needs a supported runtime without a persistent service.

Exam trap: Container technology alone does not establish the required service lifecycle.

Q Business vs. Q Developer vs. custom Bedrock

PDF trap 10 · Domain 2

Key services and controls
  • Amazon Q Business
  • Amazon Q Developer
  • Amazon Bedrock
1. Try a multiple-choice question

An organization that is an eligible existing Amazon Q Business customer wants a packaged employee assistant over supported enterprise document sources. It requires identity-aware access, built-in connectors, and conversational answers with source citations. The team prefers a managed application over building its own assistant. The sources include supported internal document repositories rather than software source-code assistance. Employees must receive only content their identity permits. There is no requirement for a bespoke business transaction workflow or GPU-serving configuration. Which service best matches this category?

  1. Configure Q Business with supported document connectors and employee identity-aware access.
  2. Configure Q Developer for employee questions and use its developer-assistance experience as the document assistant.
  3. Build a custom employee frontend and retrieval/application logic around Bedrock Knowledge Bases.
  4. Host a model on SageMaker and implement custom connectors, retrieval, permissions, and the employee frontend.
Reveal the solutionThe deciding clue

The requirement is a packaged enterprise knowledge assistant with connectors and citations. The customer is eligible to continue using the service.

Why this answer fits

A. Configure Q Business with supported document connectors and employee identity-aware access.

Amazon Q Business is the enterprise-assistant category described here. It packages the document-connector and employee question-answering experience, whereas a Bedrock application requires the team to build that experience. Q Developer addresses developer productivity rather than this employee knowledge task.

Why the alternatives fail
  1. Configure Q Developer for employee questions and use its developer-assistance experience as the document assistant.

    Q Developer is oriented to developer tasks; it is not the packaged enterprise document assistant requested.

  2. Build a custom employee frontend and retrieval/application logic around Bedrock Knowledge Bases.

    A custom Bedrock assistant can be a valid architecture, but adds application work when the scenario explicitly prefers a packaged solution.

  3. Host a model on SageMaker and implement custom connectors, retrieval, permissions, and the employee frontend.

    An endpoint still needs connectors, retrieval, identity-aware application logic, and a user experience.

What would change the answer?

Choose a custom Bedrock application when bespoke interaction or business integration requires control beyond the packaged assistant. Check current service availability before a real deployment.

How the services fit together
  1. Employee identity: establish authorized access
  2. Q Business connectors: ingest supported enterprise sources
  3. Q Business assistant: retrieve permitted evidence
  4. Employee response: answer with source citations
Read the related guide →
2. Learn the distinction

Distinguish an enterprise assistant, developer productivity, and an application you build.

Amazon Q Business

Choose when: Packaged enterprise search/chat over supported organizational sources fits.

Exam trap: Exam scope and availability for new deployments are separate questions.

Amazon Q Developer

Choose when: Developers need supported coding, review, transformation, or IDE help.

Exam trap: Developer productivity is not the employee knowledge-assistant requirement.

Custom application using Amazon Bedrock

Choose when: Custom UX, integration logic, or business workflow control is required.

Exam trap: Building the application adds responsibility and development.

SageMaker AI hosting

Choose when: Use an endpoint when model hosting controls are required.

Exam trap: Model hosting alone does not implement enterprise search and application features.

GenAI gateway vs. direct invocation

PDF trap 15 · Domain 2

Key services and controls
  • Amazon API Gateway
  • AWS Lambda
  • AWS AppConfig
  • Amazon CloudWatch / AWS Budgets
1. Try a multiple-choice question

Five teams invoke Bedrock from separate applications. The platform team must enforce team-specific model access and token admission, attribute usage to each team, and change model routes without client releases. Clients already have authenticated identities. API request-rate limits are already in place, but equal request counts produce very different token usage. A route change should be deployed once by the platform team, and clients must not be trusted to enforce their own entitlements. Which architecture most directly supplies a consistent shared enforcement point?

  1. Use a shared API Gateway/application router with trusted team identity, enforced token admission, attribution, and AppConfig model routes.
  2. Give applications direct Bedrock access and require each team to release its own entitlement, token, and routing implementation.
  3. Use tagged direct Bedrock calls and team budgets to provide attribution and notify teams when they approach spending limits.
  4. Centralize calls behind API Gateway request-rate throttles while leaving token decisions and model routes in client releases.
Reveal the solutionThe deciding clue

Several applications need centrally enforced admission, attribution, and model routing.

Why this answer fits

A. Use a shared API Gateway/application router with trusted team identity, enforced token admission, attribution, and AppConfig model routes.

Place an application gateway/router behind API Gateway and derive team policy from trusted identity. The router checks entitlement and token admission before invoking Bedrock and records attributed usage. AppConfig can provide deployed routing configuration; policy enforcement remains application logic at the shared boundary.

Why the alternatives fail
  1. Give applications direct Bedrock access and require each team to release its own entitlement, token, and routing implementation.

    This can implement policies per application, but lacks the required common enforcement boundary and routing changes independent of client releases.

  2. Use tagged direct Bedrock calls and team budgets to provide attribution and notify teams when they approach spending limits.

    Tags and budgets help attribution and spending oversight, but do not enforce per-request model entitlement or token admission.

  3. Centralize calls behind API Gateway request-rate throttles while leaving token decisions and model routes in client releases.

    Request throttles help rate control, but do not enforce token admission; client-owned routes still require client releases.

What would change the answer?

For a single trusted application without shared routing or admission requirements, direct model invocation may be the simpler sufficient path.

How the services fit together
  1. API Gateway: accept an authenticated request
  2. Shared router: derive team identity and enforce entitlement/token admission
  3. AppConfig routing configuration: select the permitted model route
  4. Amazon Bedrock invocation: record team-attributed usage
Read the related guide →
2. Learn the distinction

A gateway centralizes shared admission, routing, accounting, and policy; a direct path stays simpler when these are unnecessary.

GenAI gateway: API Gateway + Lambda/router + accounting

Choose when: Multiple applications need shared model policy and controls.

Exam trap: API request throttles and budget alerts alone are not hard token-spend enforcement.

Direct unrestricted Bedrock credentials in each client

Choose when: A simple trusted application needs no additional shared gateway boundary.

Exam trap: Direct clients can bypass centralized admission unless controls are otherwise enforced.

AWS Budgets notifications as the admission system

Choose when: Spending thresholds require notifications or supported budget actions.

Exam trap: Budget alerts are not per-request real-time token admission.

API throttling

Choose when: Use throttles to control request admission rates.

Exam trap: Request count and token consumption are different units.

Domain 3 · 20% · AI Safety, Security, and Governance

Separate content safety, access, PII location, audit evidence, governance ceilings, and threat detection.

Guardrails vs. IAM vs. Lambda validation

PDF trap 5 · Domain 3

Key services and controls
  • Amazon Bedrock Guardrails
  • AWS IAM
  • AWS Lambda / business API
1. Try a multiple-choice question

A Bedrock agent can call a refund tool implemented in Lambda. A policy allows refunds only to the authenticated customer’s account and up to that customer’s approved amount. The model can propose an account ID and amount. The proposed request is valid JSON, and the tool role can reach the refund service. However, the same role serves many customers, and an amount allowed for one customer may be unauthorized for another. Harmful-content filtering is already enabled. Which design best enforces these transaction-specific restrictions?

  1. Validate customer ownership and the approved amount in the Lambda/refund API before executing under a scoped service role.
  2. Keep the shared tool role and use a Bedrock Guardrails policy to reject refund requests outside the stated business policy.
  3. Scope the shared Lambda role to the refund API and execute schema-valid proposals under that IAM role.
  4. Include the authenticated customer policy in the agent prompt and accept proposals that satisfy the output schema.
Reveal the solutionThe deciding clue

The proposed values must be checked against trusted customer identity and approved business data for every write.

Why this answer fits

A. Validate customer ownership and the approved amount in the Lambda/refund API before executing under a scoped service role.

Validate the account and amount in the Lambda handler or authoritative refund API before executing the write. IAM should limit which resources the handler can access, and Guardrails can apply content policy, but neither replaces the customer-specific transaction checks. Treat the model’s proposal as untrusted input.

Why the alternatives fail
  1. Keep the shared tool role and use a Bedrock Guardrails policy to reject refund requests outside the stated business policy.

    Content filtering does not verify that this account belongs to this caller or that this amount is approved.

  2. Scope the shared Lambda role to the refund API and execute schema-valid proposals under that IAM role.

    An API permission grants access to an operation; it does not by itself compare proposed values with this customer’s business rules.

  3. Include the authenticated customer policy in the agent prompt and accept proposals that satisfy the output schema.

    Instructions and a valid schema cannot enforce the trusted per-transaction checks at the write boundary.

What would change the answer?

If the question concerns access to an AWS API or resource, IAM is the relevant control; if it concerns harmful generated content, Guardrails is the content-policy control.

How the services fit together
  1. Bedrock agent: propose refund parameters
  2. Lambda / refund API: verify customer, account, amount, and approval
  3. Authorized write: execute under a narrow service role
  4. Refund result: record an idempotent transaction outcome
Read the related guide →
2. Learn the distinction

Content policy, AWS permissions, and deterministic business rules are distinct controls.

Lambda / authoritative refund API

Choose when: Schemas, customer scope, amount limits, and side effects must be enforced in code.

Exam trap: A prompt instruction is not the transaction authority.

Bedrock Guardrails

Choose when: Supported content/topic/PII/grounding policies need filtering.

Exam trap: Content safety does not implement every business entitlement or money rule.

IAM permissions

Choose when: AWS service actions and resources need least-privilege access.

Exam trap: Application-specific transaction rules still need an enforcing business boundary.

Prompt instructions

Choose when: Prompts communicate expected behavior to the model.

Exam trap: Valid structure does not prove authorization or valid business values.

PII: Macie vs. Comprehend vs. Guardrails

Domain 3 PII trifecta · PDF pp. 18, 43

Key services and controls
  • Amazon Macie
  • Amazon Comprehend
  • Amazon Bedrock Guardrails
1. Try a multiple-choice question

A company stores thousands of existing documents in Amazon S3. Before selecting files for a Bedrock Knowledge Base, security needs an inventory of eligible objects containing sensitive personal information and findings it can review. No model invocation is involved in this discovery step. The team has not yet selected the ingestion files. It needs discovery findings across the stored corpus, including a review of scan coverage, rather than only redaction of strings in future chat requests. Objects use supported formats. Which service is the best fit?

  1. Run Macie discovery on eligible S3 objects, review findings and coverage, and approve files for the ingestion pipeline.
  2. Add Comprehend PII detection to generated response processing after the entire corpus has been ingested.
  3. Apply a sensitive-information Guardrail to chat inputs and outputs and retain its interaction findings.
  4. Audit S3 bucket IAM permissions and access logs before approving the existing files for ingestion.
Reveal the solutionThe deciding clue

The target is sensitive-data discovery across existing S3 objects at rest.

Why this answer fits

A. Run Macie discovery on eligible S3 objects, review findings and coverage, and approve files for the ingestion pipeline.

Use Amazon Macie to inspect eligible S3 objects and produce sensitive-data findings. Review both findings and scan coverage before approving ingestion candidates. Macie identifies data; the ingestion process must separately quarantine or sanitize files when policy requires it.

Why the alternatives fail
  1. Add Comprehend PII detection to generated response processing after the entire corpus has been ingested.

    Checking future response text does not inventory the existing S3 source objects before ingestion.

  2. Apply a sensitive-information Guardrail to chat inputs and outputs and retain its interaction findings.

    Invocation-time content checks do not perform the requested at-rest scan of the document corpus.

  3. Audit S3 bucket IAM permissions and access logs before approving the existing files for ingestion.

    Bucket permissions do not determine which stored documents contain sensitive personal data.

What would change the answer?

Use Comprehend for supported PII detection in a text-processing pipeline, or Guardrails for supported sensitive-information handling at model interaction boundaries.

How the services fit together
  1. Amazon S3: existing source objects
  2. Amazon Macie: discover sensitive data in eligible objects
  3. Security review: inspect findings and scan coverage
  4. Ingestion approval: quarantine or sanitize before indexing as required
Read the related guide →
2. Learn the distinction

First locate the sensitive data: stored S3 objects, text processing, or model input/output.

Amazon Macie

Choose when: Discover/classify sensitive information in eligible S3 objects.

Exam trap: A finding does not automatically rewrite or sanitize the object.

Amazon Comprehend

Choose when: Detect PII/entities in a text preprocessing pipeline.

Exam trap: Detection and verified redaction are separate operations.

Amazon Bedrock Guardrails

Choose when: Block/mask supported sensitive information in model interactions.

Exam trap: Inline model safety is not a scan of a whole S3 corpus.

IAM access analysis

Choose when: IAM controls who can access resources.

Exam trap: Access policy is not an inspection of object content.

CloudTrail vs. invocation logs vs. Config

Domain 3 audit trifecta · PDF pp. 19, 43

Key services and controls
  • AWS CloudTrail
  • Bedrock Model Invocation Logging
  • AWS Config
1. Try a multiple-choice question

A Bedrock application has CloudTrail enabled. After a harmful answer is reported, investigators can identify the invoking role but cannot reconstruct the actual prompt and response. Security also needs to retain the evidence under its content-log access policy. Token counts and API timestamps are available, but the actual words are not. The selected model operation supports invocation logging in the application Region. For future supported invocations, which additional configuration most directly captures the interaction content they need?

  1. Enable Bedrock Model Invocation Logging for the supported path and retain its input/output records in protected destinations.
  2. Expand CloudTrail event capture and retain model API activity with the existing principal and request metadata.
  3. Enable Config recording and retain changes to the application’s model and logging resource configurations.
  4. Retain CloudWatch input/output token metrics and correlate their timestamps with the known caller audit events.
Reveal the solutionThe deciding clue
